title: How to Export & Analyze ChatGPT Enterprise Usage Data
summary: Export ChatGPT Enterprise and Business usage data with workspace analytics CSVs, the Analytics API or the Compliance API, then analyze it by team in BI.
body_markdown:
ChatGPT Enterprise gives admins three ways to export usage data: on-demand CSV reports from workspace analytics, the Daily Usage Analytics API for automated reporting, and the Compliance API for audit logs. For adoption and cost reporting, start with the CSV export or the Analytics API. Use the Compliance API only when you need auditable records of conversations.


This guide walks through each export step by step, explains what ChatGPT Business admins can and cannot export, and shows which metrics to analyze once the data is in a spreadsheet or BI tool.


**Key takeaways**


- **CSV export:** Workspace settings > Workspace analytics > Export data. Users, GPTs, Projects and Impact survey reports, with custom date ranges of up to 12 months.
- **Analytics API:** daily ChatGPT, Codex and Work usage for recurring reports in your warehouse or BI tool, using a workspace-scoped Admin key.
- **Compliance API:** append-only JSONL logs for eDiscovery, DLP and SIEM tools. Built for audits, not adoption dashboards.
- None of these joins usage to your org chart or compares ChatGPT with Copilot, Gemini or Claude. That is the gap a cross-tool layer like[Worklytics](https://www.worklytics.co/measureai) fills, using metadata only.


## **Why Exporting ChatGPT Enterprise Usage Data Matters**


A ChatGPT Enterprise contract is typically priced per seat, which means every inactive license is a quantifiable waste line in your budget. The ChatGPT admin console shows you headline numbers, but a dashboard you cannot query is a report, not a dataset. Exporting the underlying data is what turns "we have 2,000 seats" into answers to the questions your CFO and CIO actually ask: which departments activated, whether usage is deepening or plateauing after the initial novelty period, and whether the people using ChatGPT most are the ones whose work benefits most from it.


There is also a structural reason exports matter more for AI tools than for most SaaS.


*AI adoption is uneven by nature.*


OpenAI's own analytics define power users as the top 20 percent of users by message activity who use three or more ChatGPT tools, which implies the other 80 percent are getting a fraction of the value from the same license cost. You cannot manage that skew from a summary dashboard. You need row-level data you can segment by team, tenure, and role, and that requires getting the data out.


## What ChatGPT Enterprise lets you export


OpenAI keeps reporting and audit data in separate products, and picking the right one saves weeks ([OpenAI](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/workspace-analytics) ):


- **Workspace analytics** is the aggregated dashboard: active users, messages, seats, GPTs, projects, benchmarks and Impact survey results. It exports as CSV on demand.
- **The Analytics API** returns the same kind of aggregated usage programmatically. OpenAI's unified Daily Usage Analytics API reports daily ChatGPT, Codex and Work usage, and OpenAI recommends it to automate recurring reporting and join usage with internal organizational data ([OpenAI](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/analytics-api) ).
- **The Compliance API** is the raw audit layer. It is part of the OpenAI Compliance Logs Platform, which delivers immutable, time-windowed JSONL log files, including conversation messages and admin audit, authentication and Codex logs ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/new-tools-for-chatgpt-enterprise/) ). OpenAI says to use it for security, legal and investigation work, and to use analytics, not compliance records, to measure adoption.


If your goal is adoption, cost and ROI, start with workspace analytics or the Analytics API. The Compliance API adds legal and security review to the project without adding adoption insight. If your goal is auditability or data loss prevention, the reverse is true.


Eligible workspaces also have usage views in the Global Admin Console, where admins, owners and analytics viewers can export credit use by Codex and ChatGPT, user leaderboards and usage by feature ([OpenAI release notes](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10128477-chatgpt-enterprise-and-edu-release-notes) ).


## How to export usage data from workspace analytics (CSV)


Workspace owners, admins and members with the analytics viewer role can export reports ([OpenAI](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10875114-workspace-analytics-for-chatgpt-enterprise-and-edu) ):


1. Go to **Workspace settings > Workspace analytics** (or chatgpt.com/admin/usage).
2. Select **Export data** .
3. Choose a **Data type** : Users, GPTs, Projects or Impact survey.
4. Pick a preset date range, or select **Custom** and set a start and end date. Custom ranges can cover up to 12 months.
5. Select **Generate CSV** .


The Users report is the one most teams need. It has one row per user per period, with name, email, workspace role, groups, whether the user was active, first and last active day, total messages, messages by model, and GPT, tool and project activity. That is enough to calculate activation, weekly active users and power users in a spreadsheet or BI tool such as Google Sheets, Excel, Looker or Power BI.


Three details change how you schedule pulls:


- **Freshness:** Workspace analytics is not real time. Data refreshes every 1 to 24 hours, typically within 6 to 12 hours, with a target of up to 48 hours. Pull last week's data midweek, not Monday morning.
- **Groups:** The Filter by Group option includes SCIM-managed groups and groups created in the ChatGPT UI. Clean SCIM groups upstream are what make department breakdowns possible.
- **Limits:** Exports are on demand and CSV only. Task insights (the task-type breakdown) cannot be exported yet.


OpenAI also notes that downloaded reports are identifiable organizational data, so store them under your normal access and retention policy. Give department leaders the analytics viewer role so they can pull their own numbers without full admin rights.


## How to automate exports with the Analytics API


If someone clicking Export every Monday is not a plan, use the Analytics API. OpenAI positions it for automating recurring workspace reporting, joining usage with internal organizational data and building a controlled reporting layer ([OpenAI](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/analytics-api) ).


1. Confirm that the Daily Usage Analytics endpoint is enabled for your workspace.
2. Have an owner or admin create a workspace-scoped Admin key in the Global Admin Console under **Credentials > Admin keys** ([OpenAI release notes](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10128477-chatgpt-enterprise-and-edu-release-notes) ).
3. Give the key the **enterprise.analytics.usage.read** permission. The Codex analytics scope does not grant access to this endpoint.
4. Use the[Admin API reference](https://chatgpt.com/public/admin/api-reference) for the current routes, fields and pagination, then load the daily results into your warehouse and BI tool on a schedule.


The Analytics API returns aggregated usage, not message content, so it carries the same light privacy profile as the CSV export.


## How to export data through the Compliance API


The Compliance API is for eDiscovery, DLP and SIEM tools, and OpenAI says not to use it as a productivity dashboard or to judge individual performance ([OpenAI](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/compliance-api) ). To set it up ([OpenAI Help Center](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9261474-compliance-api-for-chatgpt-enterprise-edu-and-chatgpt-for-teachers) ):


1. Ask a workspace owner or admin to create a workspace-scoped Admin key. Only a workspace owner can grant broad compliance access or the **Conversation messages** permission. Owners and admins can grant individual log categories such as audit, authentication or app logs.
2. Use the append-only compliance log stream for ongoing collection. OpenAI's download scripts (Bash and PowerShell) list and download every log file after a timestamp and write JSONL.
3. Test ingestion into a non-production SIEM or data lake, then schedule continuous collection.
4. Keep your own copy. The Compliance Logs Platform retains data for 30 days, so you need continuous downloads to keep records longer.


If you built against the old stateful conversations route, note that OpenAI removed it on June 5, 2026 in favor of the new conversation logs system.


Before you build, be clear about what you are signing up for. With the Conversation messages permission, the Compliance API returns conversation content, including prompts and outputs. Once that sits in your storage, you own the retention, access control and privacy obligations for employee conversations. In most organizations that means legal review, works council consultation in Europe and a real employee trust question. For adoption measurement, metadata is enough: message counts, timestamps, tool types and pseudonymized user IDs show adoption patterns without anyone being able to read what an employee asked ChatGPT. Worklytics explains this approach in its guide to[tracking ChatGPT Enterprise adoption without storing personal data](https://www.worklytics.co/resources/track-chatgpt-enterprise-adoption-without-storing-personal-data) .


## Exporting data from ChatGPT Business


ChatGPT Business does not have the Enterprise workspace analytics exports or the Compliance API described above. What it does have ([OpenAI Help Center](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8798634) ):


- **Usage and credits:** Workspace-level spend controls show operational metrics such as usage and credits. They do not give admins access to members' chat history.
- **Member data export:** Members cannot export their own Business workspace data from Settings > Data controls. A workspace owner can export a member's data, where the option is available, from the Members page: open the three-dot menu next to the member and select **Export data** .


If you need team-level adoption reporting, ChatGPT Enterprise is the plan with workspace analytics, CSV exports and the APIs.


## **Where the Native Exports Fall Short**


The CSV exports answer the first-order question of who used ChatGPT and how much. They stop short in four specific places, and each gap follows from what the export is not designed to contain.


**No organizational context.** The Users export identifies people, not org structure beyond your groups. To answer "how does Engineering compare to Finance," you have to join the export against your HRIS data yourself, keep that join current as people move teams, and handle the identity matching when the email in ChatGPT does not match the email in Workday. Worklytics' walkthrough on[tracking ChatGPT Enterprise usage by department without extra instrumentation](https://www.worklytics.co/resources/track-chatgpt-enterprise-usage-by-department-2025-without-instrumentation) covers why this join is the step most internal projects stall on.

**No cross-tool view.** Your organization almost certainly runs more than one AI tool. ChatGPT exports say nothing about Copilot, Gemini, Claude, or Cursor, so a team that looks inactive in your ChatGPT CSV may simply be doing the same work in a different tool. Vendor-by-vendor reporting systematically misreads substitution as non-adoption.


**No exportable work classification.** A message count treats a one-line "rewrite this email" the same as a forty-turn debugging session. OpenAI's Task insights view now groups conversations into task types inside the dashboard, but it cannot be exported yet, so you cannot join it to your own data or compare it across tools.


**No outcome linkage.** Usage data alone cannot tell you whether adoption improved anything. That requires correlating AI activity with collaboration and output signals over time, which is analytics work, not export work.


## **Analyzing the Data: The Metrics That Actually Move Decisions**


Once the data is out, resist the urge to chart everything. Four metrics carry most of the decision weight, and each maps to a specific action.


**Activation rate** (active users divided by licensed seats) is your license reallocation signal. Seats inactive after 60 days should move to waitlisted teams before renewal, because renewal negotiations price on total seats, not active ones.


**Weekly active usage frequency** distinguishes habit from experimentation. A user who sends messages five days a week has integrated the tool into their workflow. A user who spikes once a month is still deciding. The trend line matters more than the level: flattening WAU three months post-rollout is the earliest reliable signal that your enablement program has reached its ceiling.


*Depth metrics for ChatGPT in Worklytics: a user running two 12-message sessions is getting far more value than one running eight single-message lookups.*


**Power-user distribution** tells you where expertise concentrates. If your top 20 percent of users cluster in two teams, those teams hold the prompt patterns and workflows the rest of the org needs, which makes them your internal training resource. Uneven distribution is not a problem to fix, it is an asset to spread.


*Engineering and IT sit in the power-user quadrant while Sales and HR remain dabblers. Each quadrant calls for a different enablement play.*


**Category mix over time** shows whether usage is deepening. Early adoption skews toward drafting and summarization because those require no workflow change. A shift toward analysis, research, and coding indicates employees are trusting the tool with harder work. Worklytics automatically classifies AI activity into these categories (coding, research, analysis, summarization, drafting, and email creation), which is the piece raw message counts cannot give you. Its guide to[building a ChatGPT usage dashboard](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/visualize-your-chatgpt-usage-through-dashboard) shows what this looks like assembled.


*Work classification across the full AI stack: ChatGPT skews toward research and content creation while Cursor and GitHub Copilot are almost entirely code generation. This is the view native vendor exports cannot produce.*

## Frequently asked questions


### How do I export ChatGPT Enterprise usage data?


Go to Workspace settings > Workspace analytics, select Export data, choose Users, GPTs, Projects or Impact survey, pick a date range and select Generate CSV. Custom ranges can cover up to 12 months. Owners, admins and members with the analytics viewer role can export.


### Can I automate ChatGPT Enterprise usage exports?


Yes. CSV exports in the dashboard are on demand only, but the Daily Usage Analytics API reports daily ChatGPT, Codex and Work usage for recurring reporting. You need a workspace-scoped Admin key with the enterprise.analytics.usage.read permission, and the endpoint must be enabled for your workspace.


### Can I export individual conversations from ChatGPT Enterprise?


Yes, through the Compliance API, which delivers conversation messages as JSONL log files. Only a workspace owner can grant the Conversation messages permission, and logs are kept for 30 days, so you need continuous downloads. It is built for eDiscovery, DLP and SIEM tools, not adoption reporting.


### How do I export data from ChatGPT Business?


ChatGPT Business does not have the Enterprise analytics exports or the Compliance API. Workspace owners can export a member's data from the Members page, where the Export data option is available, and spend controls show usage and credits.


### How do I analyze ChatGPT usage by department?


Set up SCIM groups that match real teams so the Users export and the Filter by Group option carry department data. Then join the export to your HRIS data in a spreadsheet or BI tool, or use a tool like Worklytics that does the org join automatically and reports at the team level.
